linkedin.title: Most news algorithms get it wrong because they only look at what you click.
linkedin.body:
It is easy to assume that a click equals interest. If you open a story about a new tech gadget, the algorithm assumes you love tech gadgets. But maybe you just clicked because the headline was catchy or you were bored for a minute. That is where most personalization goes off the rails.

At Headlinne, we look at it differently. True personalization is not about tracking every single tap. It is about understanding the intent behind the reading habits you build over time. It is about separating the noise from the signal.

We built our engine to learn what actually matters to you. It pays attention to the topics you consistently return to and the depth at which you engage with them. It is less about chasing engagement metrics and more about respecting your time.

Good AI should act like a smart editor who knows your taste, not a billboard trying to sell you something you already saw yesterday.

story_card.headline: How common dust makes clouds freeze
story_card.standfirst: Scientists have found why tiny mineral particles act as seeds for ice crystals in the sky.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text: Researchers discovered how the mineral microcline triggers ice formation in clouds.

steps.label: How we got here
steps.text: Pure water usually stays liquid until it hits -38°C. Dust particles help it freeze sooner.

steps.label: Why it matters
steps.text: Understanding these ice nucleators helps us track how clouds form and change our weather.

steps.label: What to watch
steps.text: Future studies will explore how other mineral dust types affect cloud behavior.

story_card.caption:
Scientists at Bielefeld University have identified how the mineral microcline helps clouds form ice crystals.

Pure water is stubborn and doesn't freeze until it reaches extreme cold. Tiny particles of dust act as a shortcut, giving ice a surface to grow on at warmer temperatures. This research helps us understand the complex physics happening high above our heads.
